title: Southern Cutgrass in Rice Fields: How to Spot and Remove It
metaTitle: Southern Cutgrass in Rice: Identify It and Dig It Out
metaDescription: Southern cutgrass is a perennial grass that roots at its joints and returns from its rootstocks. Learn how to spot it and clear it from your palay.
excerpt: Southern cutgrass is a creeping perennial grass weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Its leaves carry tiny backward spines that feel rough and can scratch your skin. This page shows how to spot it, how it hurts your palay and how to keep it in check, season after season.

blocks.text:
Southern cutgrass (Leersia hexandra) belongs to the grass family, the same family as palay. Farmers call it amgid or barit. It grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields, and it handles wet, flooded ground well. Its stems rise at an angle or stand almost upright, and they root wherever a joint touches wet soil.

This weed is a perennial, so it does not die after one season. It spreads by seed and also by its rootstocks, the stems that run under the soil and store food. When you plow or pull it, broken pieces of rootstock stay in the mud. Each piece can grow into a new plant. That is why a small patch keeps growing if you only cut the tops.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about southern cutgrass
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like other grasses, it has round, hollow stems with clear joints, or nodes. The stems rise at an angle or stand almost straight, and they root at the nodes. The leaves are long and narrow, tapering to a fine point. Now run your fingers along the midrib on the back of a leaf. You will feel tiny spines that point backward and catch your skin. The ligule is long, thin and rounded. The seed head has slender branches and oblong spikelets.

items: Stems lean up at an angle or stand almost straight, rooting at the joints.
Leaves are long and narrow, and each one ends in a fine, tapering point.
Tiny backward pointing spines line the back of the midrib and catch your skin.
The ligule is long and thin, with a rounded tip.
Slender seed head branches stand nearly upright and carry oblong spikelets.
Patches come back in the same spots season after season from old rootstocks.

blocks.text:
As a perennial, this grass does not wait for a new season to start. Old rootstocks are often still alive when you plant, so it starts taking water, light and fertilizer from your palay right away. Its rooting stems also knit into thick mats that crowd young rice hills.

It costs you labor too. Pulling the tops does little, because the rootstocks send up new shoots. So weeding by hand takes longer, and the rough leaves scratch the hands that pull them. Besides that, thick patches can give rice pests shelter between crops. Its seeds may also end up mixed with your harvest.

items: Dig out each clump with its rootstocks during land preparation. Any piece you leave in the mud can sprout again.
After plowing, rake the broken rootstock pieces out of the paddy and dry them on high ground, not on the bund.
Flooding alone will not stop it, because this grass grows well in wet ground. Rely on digging and careful land preparation instead.
Wear gloves and long sleeves when you weed it, since the tiny spines on its leaves can cut your skin.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Grasses

If water and weeding cannot hold southern cutgrass down, choose an active ingredient that works on grasses at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Southern Cutgrass Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before the seed heads open, and clean the thresher and harvester before they enter the field.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [grass weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Southern Cutgrass

items.q: What do farmers call southern cutgrass locally?
items.a: Farmers call it amgid or barit. Its scientific name is Leersia hexandra. Be careful with barit, because the same name also goes to knotgrass in some places. To be sure, run your fingers along the back of a leaf. This grass has tiny backward spines on the midrib that catch your skin, and its stems root at the joints.

items.q: How do I get rid of it in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention starts at land preparation. Dig out clumps with their rootstocks, rake out broken pieces and keep the bunds and canals clean. Water alone will not drown it, so hand weed and dig early while patches are small. If you need a herbicide, choose one for grass weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does southern cutgrass keep coming back?
items.a: Because it is a perennial with rootstocks under the soil. When you cut or pull only the leaves, the rootstocks stay alive and send up new shoots. Plowing can also break them into pieces, and each piece can grow into a new plant. So dig out the whole clump, carry the pieces out of the field, and check the spot again after a few weeks.
